sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: GORM is the most widely-used ORM in the Go ecosystem and frequently appears in production codebases. Interviewers want to see that you can use it productively while understanding its hidden costs — N+1 queries, silent error swallowing, and reflection-based scanning. Ent, from Meta, represents a schema-first, code-generated alternative that is gaining traction for type-safe, graph-shaped data access. Being able to compare both tools intelligently, and knowing when raw sql/sqlx is the better choice, marks you as an experienced Go engineer rather than someone who always reaches for the same hammer.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: GORM builds SQL statements lazily through a chain of method calls on *gorm.DB. Each method (Where, Order, Limit) returns a new *gorm.DB scope; the actual query is only sent to the database when a terminal method (Find, First, Create, Save, Delete) is called. gorm.Model embeds ID, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, DeletedAt giving you soft-deletes by default. Associations (HasMany, BelongsTo) are resolved via Preload (separate SELECT) or Joins (JOIN). Hooks (BeforeCreate, AfterSave) inject business logic into the ORM lifecycle. Ent flips the model: you define an ent/schema in Go code, run go generate to emit a fully type-safe, query-builder client — no reflection, compile-time checked field names.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. gorm.Model vs plain struct — gorm.Model adds soft-delete; plain structs give you explicit control. 2. Preload vs Joins — Preload fires a second SELECT (N+1 risk on collections), Joins uses a SQL JOIN (one query, but cartesian row expansion). 3. Hooks — BeforeCreate, AfterCreate, BeforeUpdate, AfterUpdate, BeforeDelete; return an error to abort the operation. 4. AutoMigrate — convenient in development, dangerous in production; prefer versioned migration tools (golang-migrate, Atlas). 5. Raw SQL via gorm.Raw / Exec — always available as an escape hatch. 6. Error handling — GORM returns errors on the *gorm.DB.Error field; always check it after terminal methods. 7. Ent schema — define entity shape in ent/schema/user.go with Fields() and Edges(); go generate produces a full type-safe client. 8. Ent Edges — model graph relationships with From/To, replacing foreign-key juggling.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: How does GORM's Preload lead to an N+1 problem? — For each parent record GORM issues a separate SELECT for related children; with 100 orders you get 101 queries. Fix with Preload batching or Joins. Q: What is GORM's soft-delete mechanism? — DeletedAt is set to the current timestamp rather than deleting the row; queries automatically filter WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Q: When would you choose Ent over GORM? — When type safety and compile-time checked queries matter more than convention-over-configuration, or when the data model is highly relational/graph-shaped. Q: Why is AutoMigrate risky in production? — It can add columns but never removes them; it cannot handle complex migrations like column renames, index changes, or data backfills. Q: How do you call a stored procedure or raw SQL in GORM? — db.Raw("SELECT ...", args...).Scan(&result) or db.Exec("CALL proc(...)", args...).

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I use GORM for standard CRUD-heavy services where developer velocity matters — the convention-based approach means less boilerplate. But I always benchmark Preload vs Joins for any query that touches associations on a list endpoint, because Preload is a silent N+1 waiting to happen. I never use AutoMigrate in production; instead I version migrations with golang-migrate and run them as a job before the new service version starts. For services with complex, graph-shaped domains — like a billing or permissions system — I lean toward Ent because the code-generated client gives us compile-time guarantees that raw GORM struct tags can't match. In either case I keep GORM's Raw/Exec as a first-class option for reporting queries or CTEs that the ORM generates poorly."
